label: D’Arcy McNickle
description: A writer, administrator and historian, an enrolled member at Flathead (Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes), per Iverson 1993. He helped found the National Congress of American Indians (1944), organised the Workshops on American Indian Affairs from 1960, and chaired the steering committee of the 1961 Chicago conference. They Came Here First (1949) and Native American Tribalism (1973) argued against 'the certainty that native America had vanished before the march of progress': Congress in the 1950s had judged that 'Indians had no future as Indians', and termination tried 'to legislate Indians out of existence'. In 1972 he helped create the Newberry Library's centre for Indian history and directed it in its first fellowship year (1973–74). Iverson (1993) noted that 'few Native historians have tried to provide an overview of the national Indian experience'. Vine Deloria Jr. criticised the workshops' approach in 1965.

label: Aldo Leopold
description: A forester, wildlife ecologist and conservationist, not a historian, whose posthumous A Sand County Almanac (1949) set out a 'land ethic' that 'changes the role of Homo sapiens from conqueror of the land-community to plain member and citizen of it'. In the same essay he wrote that an 'ecological interpretation of history' shows that 'many historical events, hitherto explained solely in terms of human enterprise, were actually biotic interactions between people and land', and took as his example the Kentucky canelands that became bluegrass under 'the cow, plow, fire, and axe of the pioneer'. He asked: 'Is history taught in this spirit? It will be, once the concept of land as a community really penetrates our intellectual life.' Environmental historians later cited the call: Worster (1988) wrote that Leopold 'projected such an alliance' between history and ecology, and Cronon (1993) described the field's subject as 'the history recorded in Aldo Leopold’s tree rings'.
date_label: Land ethic and ecological interpretation of history · A Sand County Almanac 1949
representative_figures_and_works: Aldo Leopold (1887–1948); A Sand County Almanac, and Sketches Here and There (1949), especially 'Good Oak' and 'The Land Ethic'. Readings: Nash, Wilderness and the American Mind (1967), chapter 'Aldo Leopold: Prophet'; Worster, 'Doing Environmental History' (1988) and 'Transformations of the Earth' (1990); Cronon, 'The Uses of Environmental History' (1993) and History 901 syllabus (1994). Later readings: Wynn (2001); MacEachern (2002); Cronon's afterword to Changes in the Land (2003).
scope_note: This entry presents Leopold as a precursor whose writing environmental historians cited, not as a historian and not as the founder of environmental history. 'The Land Ethic' and 'Good Oak' are read in two unpaginated transcriptions (the 1966 enlarged Oxford text and an excerpt of the 1949 essay); the 1949 page of the history passage (p. 205) is the one Worster (1990, n. 1) and Wynn (2001, n. 55) both cite. Worster's 1988 essay dates 'the idea of environmental history' to the 1970s, the global-predicament conferences and the environmental movement, not to Leopold. His 1990 essay, read only in Portuguese translation, cautions that the Kentucky case is more complicated than Leopold's example and needs more than a simple environmental determinism, and adds that bluegrass was a European import, which Leopold had said was not known. Cronon's 1993 uses are echoes of a moral and literary voice, not a borrowed method. Canadian writing differs: MacEachern (2002, p. 219) faults a history of Ontario conservation for assuming, without evidence, that Leopold 'was being read by Canadians, let alone influencing them' (a remark about naturalists of the 1950s, not about historians), and Wynn (2001, p. 145), a historical geographer, urges geographers to 'respond to Leopold’s call' and observes: 'Few have done so'.

edges.relationship: Environmental historians cite Leopold's call for 'an ecological interpretation of history' (1949) as a precedent for allying history with ecology, and his essays as a moral and literary voice

Leopold as teacher and model: the landscape-reading course he drew from Leopold (afterword, 2003), essays on Leopold and A Sand County Almanac (1998), and Leopold among the 'Classics and Precursors' of his reading list (2005)

label: Rachel Carson
description: A marine biologist and science writer whose Silent Spring (1962) was a catalyst for environmental concern and became a shared text for US environmental historians; it is not a work of history. The book argued that 'the central problem of our age has therefore become the contamination of man’s total environment' by persistent chemicals, followed pesticides through 'the web of life — or death — that scientists know as ecology', and called the 'control of nature' 'a phrase conceived in arrogance'. It did not reject all control: 'control must be geared to realities, not to mythical situations'. Historians who shaped the field took the book up as a starting point: John Opie's 1971 reader opens 'The Contemporary Controversy Begins' with her, and Donald Worster's history of ecological ideas (1977) places Silent Spring near the opening of 'The Age of Ecology'.

scope_note: A precursor entry for a catalyst of environmental concern, not a historian. Silent Spring is quoted from the 2002 Mariner edition (a partial scan was read: pp. 1–9, 172–198, 278–279 and 296–297, with Lear's introduction); Worster's 1977 notes cite pp. 8 and 297 for the same sentences, so the pagination matches the 1962 edition at those points. She is not presented as a founder or as the catalyst of environmental history as a discipline. Worster (1977; Internet Archive full-text search, page located by the index) credits her with launching the recent ecology movement, which is the movement, not the field. The disciplinary claim is a later, geographically qualified reading: Carruthers (2004) reports that Grove conceded Silent Spring's importance to the discipline only for the United States. The Canadian self-accounts read for this batch name her as 1960s context, not as a model. The book was contested from the start. Velsicol's general counsel attributed attacks on the chemical industry to sinister influences (his letter as quoted by Graham, 1970, in Opie's reader, p. 93 from a running head). Dunlap (1981, pp. 3–4 and 7 from running heads) records that defenders of DDT condemned her as a crank, and judges that she had done no original research. Nash (1989, p. 80 from a running head) finds much traditional anthropocentrism in her ethics. These three are known only through Internet Archive full-text search of borrow-only scans (page images not seen), so they are paraphrased. Lear (2002), a later reading, writes that the cancer evidence still fuels an 'acrimonious' debate. The 1962 reviews in Science (Baldwin) and Time were not read.

label: Anthony Giddens
description: Develops structuration as an account of how social practices reproduce and transform the rules and resources on which they depend. Structure is both enabling and constraining, not merely an outside force confronting a free individual. The selected chapter also makes time and space constitutive of social practice: purposeful conduct unfolds through embodied, situated activity, and its consequences exceed what actors intend. This avoids treating either an individual subject or a social whole as a self-sufficient starting point. The earlier Sewell abstract identifies a later reformulation, while its limited reading does not establish every detail of that criticism.

label: Robert Alexander Innes
description: Cowessess First Nation historian of kinship and treaty land, and a critic of how historians have written the 1880s starvation policy. In 2018 he wrote that neither historians nor the Canadian government had acknowledged the starvation deaths of the early 1880s in Treaty 4 territory as genocide, and that historians who agreed the policy killed many had not tried to count the dead. Cowessess First Nation's own treaty land entitlement research had done that work. Historical records, he argued, do not tell a story by themselves, and decolonizing history can simply mean asking the right questions and looking in the right places. Against Daschuk's Clearing the Plains (2013), he held that Edgar Dewdney bore responsibility and that Daschuk misrepresented Tobias, Lux and Titley, whom he cites. Earlier he wrote on oral history methods in Native Studies and on insider research; he conceived Shekon Neechie (2018).

label: Barbara H. Rosenwein
description: A medieval historian whose studies of property, immunity and power led to an influential approach to the history of emotions. ‘Worrying about Emotions in History’ (2002) revisits Lucien Febvre’s call for a history of feeling and rejects the grand narrative, associated with Norbert Elias, of a movement from unrestrained medieval emotion to modern self-control. In a 2010 interview she questions William Reddy’s sharp distinction between emotional regimes and emotional refuges; Reddy’s reply allowing plural regimes stands beside her objection. Emotional Communities in the Early Middle Ages (2006) is the book-length study.

label: Jonathan Israel
description: A historian of the Dutch Republic, European Jewry and the Enlightenment whose radical-Enlightenment interpretation gives philosophical ideas a strong explanatory role. In a 2023 interview, Israel argues that the reception of Spinoza helped create a radical current committed to secularism, democratic republicanism and freedom of expression, which he opposes to a moderate Enlightenment. David Bell credits Israel’s range and his insistence on ideas, but argues that he infers influence from similarity, takes passages out of context and overstates the ideological causes of the French Revolution.

label: E. H. Carr
description: A historian of Soviet Russia and of international relations whose What Is History? (1961) became the standard British introduction to historical method. Carr argued that historians select and give meaning to facts through their questions, so that research and interpretation proceed together; his position was long read as a challenge to objectivist history. G. R. Elton’s The Practice of History (1967) was written in open opposition, and John Tosh called the Carr–Elton controversy the best starting point for debate about the standing of historical knowledge. Richard Evans wrote In Defence of History (1997) because Carr’s and Elton’s books were still the standard textbooks and, in his view, inadequate for later debates. The Twenty Years’ Crisis (1939) belongs to his work on international relations, and his History of Soviet Russia began with The Bolshevik Revolution (1950).

label: Sheila Fitzpatrick
description: A historian of the Soviet Union and of Stalinism from below. In ‘Revisionism in Retrospect’ (2008) she gives a participant’s account of how social historians of the 1970s and 1980s challenged political scientists’ totalitarian model, crediting revisionism with an appreciation of contingency and a new approach to power and to the interplay of government and society. label: Paul Thompson
description: A social and oral historian concerned with how interviews change both historical evidence and research practice. His retrospective interview credits Townsend’s socially engaged research and George Ewart Evans’s listening methods, and recalls resisting Hobsbawm’s request to remove oral-history material from The Edwardians. Thompson distinguishes his early emphasis on reliable recollection from later attention to subjectivity, silence and memory associated with Passerini and Portelli. His community-history discussion also warns that participation can exclude less confident people and need not produce progressive politics. Becky Taylor’s reassessment credits the fishing project’s attention to change and its preservation of sources, while questioning interview schedules, uneven transcription and the insufficiently examined category of fisherman. Her reuse demonstrates how an archive can support questions its makers did not fully pursue. label: Charles E. Rosenberg
description: A historian of medicine and science. The Cholera Years (1962), on the United States in 1832, 1849 and 1866, is credited with leading historians to study not only a disease and its victims but society’s response to it, through politics, law and social mores. The Care of Strangers (1987), a history of the American hospital, and Explaining Epidemics (1992) continued that social history of medicine. In a 2013 interview he places his work within a social-medicine tradition that treats medical ideas and access to care as embedded in society, questions tidy genealogies in which translated theorists alone changed historical research, and distinguishes psychiatric diagnostic categories that organize research and care from explanations of mechanism.

label: Robert Bartlett
description: A medieval historian of conquest, law and historical categories. Trial by Fire and Water (1986) studied the medieval judicial ordeal, and The Making of Europe (1993) traced conquest, colonization and cultural change between 950 and 1350. His 2001 article on race and ethnicity treats both terms as social constructions and warns against using present administrative labels as ready-made historical explanations. Comparing medieval terminology, he emphasizes culture, law, language and religion in the making of identities, while examining genealogical idioms of descent, and separates collective identity from any automatic demand for sovereign statehood. Geraldine Heng later questions the sharpness of his distinction between medieval cultural difference and biological racism.
